Title: A hybrid framework for heart disease prediction using classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques
Author: Ankur Kumar; Sanjay Dhanka; Abhinav Sharma; Rohit Bansal; Mochammad Fahlevi; Fazla Rabby; Mohammed Aljuaid
Abstract: This research proposes a hybrid framework integrating classical and quantum-inspired machine learning techniques to enhance heart disease prediction. Using a combined UCI dataset and preprocessing/feature selection, the study trains and optimizes both classical and quantum-inspired SVM-based models evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
Method Used: Classical pipeline: CGA + CPSO + CSVM. Quantum-inspired pipeline (simulated): QGA + QPSO + QSVM using Qiskit Aer simulator.
Result: Quantum-inspired model: accuracy 97.83%, sensitivity 98.96%, specificity 96.59%, F1 97.94%, AUC 97%. Classical model: accuracy 94.02%. Runtime: 413.57s (quantum) vs 362.92s (classical).
Conclusion: Quantum-inspired hybrid outperformed classical hybrid across metrics while using fewer features; higher computational cost; demonstrated via classical simulation only.
Limitations: Quantum methods on classical simulators (not real QPU); increased runtime; no external validation on larger datasets; hardware noise/coherence constraints remain.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, AUC, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A primer for quantum computing and its applications to healthcare and biomedical research
Author: Thomas J.S. Durant; Elizabeth Knight; Brent Nelson; Sarah Dudgeon; Seung J. Lee; Dominic Walliman; Hobart P. Young; Lucila Ohno-Machado; Wade L. Schulz
Abstract: Introduces quantum computing technologies for biomedical research and highlights future applications in healthcare focusing on capabilities, benefits, limitations, and current state of hardware/software.
Method Used: Narrative literature review / primer — no original experimental model.
Result: Summarizes current quantum hardware is limited; QPUs should be viewed as accelerators complementary to CPUs/GPUs; practical quantum advantage for real-world biomedical tasks remains limited.
Conclusion: Quantum computing has promising potential for high-complexity biomedical problems but real-world advantages not yet broadly demonstrated; depends on hardware maturity and clearer benchmarking.
Limitations: Not a primary experimental study; conclusions depend on available literature; many cited applications constrained by current device scale/noise.

Title: A Quantum-Enhanced Precision Medicine Application to Support Data-Driven Clinical Decisions for the Personalized Treatment of Advanced Knee Osteoarthritis
Author: Nima Heidari; Stefano Olgiati; Davide Meloni; Mark Slevin; Ali Noorani; Federico Pirovano; Leonard Azamfirei
Abstract: QNN application to support precision data-driven clinical decisions to select personalized treatments for advanced knee osteoarthritis by classifying treatment responders vs non-responders.
Method Used: QNN (parameterized quantum circuit; Qiskit OpflowQNN); COBYLA optimizer; Aer simulator 1024 shots; train/test split 113/57.
Result: Test set (n=57): sensitivity 0.8235; specificity 0.2609; F1 0.7088; LR+ 1.1142; DOR 2.0. No information rate 0.59.
Conclusion: Preliminary validation suggests QML decision support for personalized treatment selection is promising but performance (especially specificity) is limited; requires larger datasets and clinical validation.
Limitations: Small validation dataset; low specificity/high false positives; outliers handling may affect generalizability; external validation required.
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Sensitivity, Specificity, F1, LR+, LR-, DOR

Title: A quantum-optimized approach for breast cancer detection using SqueezeNet-SVM
Author: Anas Bilal; Ali Alkhathlan; Faris A. Kateb; Alishba Tahir; Muhammad Shafiq; Haixia Long
Abstract: Proposes a hybrid approach Q-BGWO-SQSVM using quantum-inspired binary Grey Wolf Optimizer with SqueezeNet and SVM to enhance breast cancer classification accuracy.
Method Used: Mammogram preprocessing + Otsu thresholding segmentation + SqueezeNet feature extraction + SVM with Q-BGWO hyperparameter optimization; 5/10/15-fold CV on MIAS, INbreast, DDSM, CBIS-DDSM.
Result: Best on CBIS-DDSM with 15-fold CV: accuracy 99%, sensitivity 98%, specificity 100%.
Conclusion: Q-BGWO-SQSVM achieves near state-of-the-art mammography classification; reliable efficient approach for early breast cancer detection; further validation recommended.
Limitations: Reliance on benchmark datasets and cross-validation; clinical real-world deployment not validated; performance depends on preprocessing/ROI selection.
Classical Baseline Quality: Unclear — compared to prior literature only

Title: A systematic review of quantum machine learning for digital health
Author: Riddhi S. Gupta; Carolyn E. Wood; Teyl Engstrom; Jason D. Pole; Sally Shrapnel
Abstract: Systematic review assessing whether QML algorithms outperform existing classical methods for clinical decisioning or health service delivery. 4915 initial records; 169 eligible; 46 high-quality; 16 with realistic operating conditions.
Method Used: Systematic review (PRISMA; SPICE; PROSPERO); searched PubMed/Embase/IEEE/Scopus/arXiv 2015-2024; quality appraisal to 46 high-quality studies.
Result: No consistent empirical performance advantage of QML over classical methods in digital health; most studies rely on ideal simulations; only 16 used realistic operating conditions.
Conclusion: Current evidence base insufficient to claim empirical quantum utility in digital health; future work must establish scalability, uncertainty, noise robustness, and stronger benchmarking.
Limitations: Many studies excluded for low technical rigor; heterogeneous metrics impede meta-analysis; limited use of EHR/real-world datasets.

Title: A unifying nonlinear probabilistic epidemic model in space and time
Author: Roberto Beneduci; Eleonora Bilotta; Pietro Pantano
Abstract: Proposes a continuous space-time nonlinear probabilistic mother model for epidemic spread based on sub-probability densities; shows how multiple deterministic and stochastic epidemic models can be derived as special cases.
Method Used: Defines infected and susceptible sub-probability densities; derives coupled integro-differential equations; under locality/symmetry assumptions derives generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov-type drift-diffusion PDE; discretizes to obtain discrete stochastic processes.
Result: Key derivations: evolution equations for infected/susceptible densities; generalized Fisher-Kolmogorov with anomalous diffusion; classical Fisher-Kolmogorov arises from linearized probabilistic model.
Conclusion: Provides a unifying probabilistic framework connecting stochastic and deterministic epidemic models; forecasting applications depend on estimating kernel W from data.
Limitations: Assumes existence and differentiability of sub-probability densities; no births/deaths in base formulation; practical use depends on solving inverse problem to estimate kernel W from data.

Title: Advancing single-cell omics and cell-based therapeutics with quantum computing
Author: Aritra Bose; Kahn Rhrissorrakrai; Filippo Utro; Laxmi Parida; Quantum for Healthcare Life Sciences Consortium
Abstract: Roadmap article discussing how quantum computing could complement AI to address computational bottlenecks in spatiotemporal single-cell and spatial omics analysis.
Method Used: Narrative roadmap/review of quantum computing analogues for key single-cell/spatial analysis tasks; no new validated model.
Result: Not reported — roadmap only.
Conclusion: Quantum computing may help overcome scaling, generalization, and sample-limited challenges in single-cell/spatial multi-omics; near-term utility depends on hardware maturity and careful benchmarking.
Limitations: Not yet clinically validated; many proposed approaches require fault-tolerant devices; major practical hurdles include data encoding overhead, noise/coherence limits, barren plateaus.

Title: An integrated strategy based on radiomics and quantum machine learning: diagnosis and clinical interpretation of pulmonary ground-glass nodules
Author: Xianzhi Huang; Fangyi Xu; Wenchao Zhu; Lin Yao; Jiahuan He; Junhao Su; Wending Zhao; Hongjie Hu
Abstract: Retrospective study developing integrated pipeline combining CT radiomics and QML (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) with SHAP interpretability to classify pulmonary pGGNs as invasive vs non-invasive adenocarcinoma.
Method Used: CT pGGN segmentation + radiomics extraction (960 features) + Random Forest feature selection (9 features) + QML models (QSVC, Pegasos QSVC, QNN) on Qiskit noiseless simulator; SHAP interpretability.
Result: QNN: accuracy 89.23% (95% CI 81.54-95.38), sensitivity 96.55%, specificity 83.33%, AUC 0.937. QNN AUC significantly outperformed classical SVM AUC 0.833 (p=0.003).
Conclusion: Integrated radiomics + QML + SHAP improves pGGN invasiveness classification vs classical SVM; QNN performed best; supports use as non-invasive decision-support tool.
Limitations: Single-center retrospective design; relatively small sample; radiomics sensitive to scan parameters; SHAP visualization largely qualitative; scalability constrained by current quantum hardware.

Title: Applications of quantum computing in clinical care
Author: Stevan C. Fairburn; Lara Jehi; Brenton T. Bicknell; Beckley G. Wilkes; Bharat Panuganti
Abstract: Systematic review of quantum computing applications with first-order clinical relevance; summarizes evidence for impacts on diagnostics, treatment optimization, and real-time decision support.
Method Used: Systematic review across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science (Jan 2015-Jan 2024); screened 237 records; included 35 studies; thematic synthesis.
Result: QC promise across medical imaging and clinical decision-making (each 54.3% of included articles) and oncology (48.6%); many studies theoretical/simulation-based or use synthetic data.
Conclusion: Quantum computing shows potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy and computational efficiency; clinical adoption limited by current technical, validation, and ethical constraints.
Limitations: Limited database scope; most included work theoretical/simulator-based/synthetic; heterogeneity limits generalizability; potential publication bias; lack of standardized benchmarks.

Title: Biology and medicine in the landscape of quantum advantages
Author: Benjamin A. Cordier; Nicolas P. D. Sawaya; Gian Giacomo Guerreschi; Shannon K. McWeeney
Abstract: Review proposing framework to define and classify quantum advantage and applying it across biology/medicine problems to assess where practical advantages may emerge.
Method Used: Narrative review + conceptual framework; surveys quantum algorithms and maps them to biomedical tasks; discusses practical constraints (NISQ vs FTQC).
Result: No new experimental results; quantum simulation (VQE) identified as most promising near-to-medium-term candidate; variational QML may offer potential benefits but requires further validation.
Conclusion: Quantum simulation for molecular systems is highlighted as the clearest near-term path to meaningful quantum advantage in biomedicine; variational/hybrid methods are key near-term strategy.
Limitations: No empirical data; theoretical framework only; timeline for operational advantage uncertain.

Title: Quantum-assisted federated intelligent diagnosis algorithm with variational training supported by 5G networks
Author: Arnaldo Rafael Camara Araujo; Ogobuchi Daniel Okey; Muhammad Saadi; Pablo Adasme; Renata Lopes Rosa; Demóstenes Zegarra Rodríguez
Abstract: Proposes β-QuAFIDA: a quantum-assisted federated learning framework for intelligent healthcare diagnosis via IoMT devices connected through 5G networks. Uses β-VQE optimization in a nested loop structure to preserve privacy and improve convergence.
Method Used: β-QuAFIDA: inner loop trains β-VQE to approximate expectation values; outer loop minimizes relative entropy to target. Implemented using PennyLane + PyTorch + QuEST simulator. Angle encoding. Tested on Fetal Health Dataset (2126 CTG records); 80/20 split.
Result: Central trained VQNN: test accuracy 83.90%. β-QuAFIDA (2 clients): 83.98%; (4 clients): 84.13%; (8 clients): 83.75%. Fidelity under noise: BF=0.9958, AD=0.9775, DN=0.9993. Personalized vs no personalized training: marginal gains.
Conclusion: β-QuAFIDA demonstrates robustness in noisy NISQ environments and suitable for privacy-preserving federated diagnosis; performance consistent across distributed configurations; promising for intelligent healthcare in 5G networks.
Limitations: Sensitivity to heuristic parameters R and α; tested on single dataset; no comparison to classical federated learning baselines; scalability to larger datasets not demonstrated; all quantum components simulated.
Classical Baseline Quality: No — no classical FL baseline reported

Title: IoT driven smart health monitoring for heart disease prediction using quantum kernel enhanced sardine diffusion and CNN
Author: Dibas Kumar Hembram; Satya Narayan Tripathy; CH Narsimha Reddy; Debabrata Dansana; Quadri Noorulhasan Naveed; Shafat khan; Mohammed Kareemullah; Addisu Frinjo Emma
Abstract: Proposes IoT-based Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet for real-time heart disease prediction combining quantum clustering, Q2CNN, diffusion kernel attention, and Sardine Optimization Algorithm.
Method Used: Quantum Clustering with k-Means → Z-score Min-Max Normalization → Fast Point Transformer feature extraction → Q2CNN + DKAN (Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet) with Sardine Optimization. UCI Heart Failure dataset (299 records). 70/15/15 split.
Result: Accuracy 99.97-99.98%; Precision 99.34-99.59%; Recall 98.47-99.56%; F1 96.34-99.46%; MSE 0.01; Specificity 99.27%; Training accuracy 99.9%; Execution time 0.1s.
Conclusion: Qua-KSar-DCK-ArNet achieves impressive 99% accuracy enabling real-time IoT-based diagnosis; future work to integrate additional physiological parameters and address scalability.
Limitations: Extremely small dataset (299 records); no confidence intervals; quantum components simulated not real hardware; no strong classical DNN baseline; 99%+ accuracy on 299-record dataset is unreliable indicator of generalizable performance.
Classical Baseline Quality: Weak — compared to non-DNN baselines only
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1, MSE, Specificity
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes — claimed but dataset too small to establish

Title: Variational quantum classifier-based early identification and classification of chronic kidney disease using sparse autoencoder and LASSO shrinkage
Author: P. Parthasarathi; Haya Mesfer Alshahrani; K. Venkatachalam; Jaehyuk Cho
Abstract: QML-based technique for early diagnosis and prognosis of CKD using VQC with sparse autoencoder data augmentation and LASSO feature selection. Evaluated on UCI CKD dataset (400 patients, 25 attributes).
Method Used: Phase 1: Kalman filter + min-max normalization. Phase 2: Sparse autoencoder augmentation (KL divergence + L1). Phase 3: LASSO shrinkage (13 features selected). Phase 4: VQC (Qiskit RawFeatureVector + RealAmplitudes ansatz 3 layers + COBYLA + CrossEntropy loss).
Result: With LASSO: VQC accuracy 99.2%, precision 98.3%, recall 98.5%, F1 98.9%, AUC-ROC 99.1%. Without LASSO: VQC accuracy 98.2%. Outperforms SVM (92.8%), RF (90.7%), LR (93.9%), MLP (94.8%), QSVM (97.8%).
Conclusion: VQC with LASSO feature selection achieves 99.2% accuracy for CKD classification surpassing classical and quantum baselines; establishes groundwork for quantum-assisted medical AI systems.
Limitations: Quantum circuits susceptible to noise; scalability restricted by qubit/gate complexity; data encoding overhead; increased training time vs classical; tested only on UCI CKD dataset; no confidence intervals reported.
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes — SVM / RF / LR / MLP / QSVM compared
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes — outperforms all baselines on simulator

Title: Deep Ensemble learning and quantum machine learning approach for Alzheimer's disease detection
Author: Abebech Jenber Belay; Yelkal Mulualem Walle; Melaku Bitew Haile
Abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease threatening global public health. This study proposes a deep ensemble learning pipeline combining VGG16 and ResNet50 for feature extraction from ADNI MRI images combined with a 5-qubit Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) for 4-class AD stage classification (CN, EMCI, MCI, AD).
Method Used: Merge ADNI1+ADNI2 MRI images; preprocess (crop, resize 128x128, filtering, augmentation); extract and concatenate deep features via customized VGG16 and ResNet50; encode features using 5-qubit QSVM for 4-class classification; compare against classical SVM and end-to-end ensemble baselines
Result: VGGNet+ResNet+QSVM: Accuracy 99.89%, Precision 99.25%, Recall 99.23%, F1 99.13%, AUC 99.99%; VGGNet+QSVM: 95.65%; ResNet+QSVM: 91.56%; Ensemble+classical SVM: 86.78%; End-to-end Ensemble DL: 90.58%
Conclusion: Ensemble deep feature extraction combined with QSVM markedly improves 4-class AD stage classification over classical SVM and end-to-end DL baselines; suggests quantum ML can enhance classification accuracy in neurological medical imaging tasks
Limitations: Quantum hardware vs simulator not clearly specified beyond 5-qubit; uses Kaggle-derived ADNI subsets; resized 2D images may limit generalizability; single dataset limits external validation
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – classical SVM and end-to-end DL compared
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes – outperforms classical SVM and DL baselines

Title: Clinical data classification with noisy intermediate scale quantum computers
Author: S. Moradi; C. Brandner; C. Spielvogel; D. Krajnc; S. Hillmich; R. Wille; W. Drexler; L. Papp
Abstract: This work investigates the feasibility of quantum machine learning (QML) on real clinical datasets using NISQ devices. Two QML algorithms are proposed: a quantum distance classifier (qDC) and a simplified quantum-kernel SVM (sqKSVM) using log2N linear time encoding on the 15-qubit IBMQ Melbourne device. Three open-access clinical datasets are used: Pediatric Bone Marrow Transplant (n=134), Wisconsin Breast Cancer (n=569), and Heart Failure Mortality (n=300).
Method Used: Quantum distance classifier (qDC) and simplified quantum-kernel SVM (sqKSVM); log2N linear time encoding on 15-qubit IBMQ Melbourne real QPU; 5-fold cross-validation; compared against classical SVM and KNN
Result: qDC outperforms kernel-based methods in small sample/feature datasets; sqKSVM outperforms qDC in high sample/feature datasets; log2N encoding improves AUC by up to +2% across all QML approaches
Conclusion: QML on NISQ hardware achieves comparable performance to classical methods on clinical datasets; log2N encoding is efficient for small-qubit devices; dataset size determines which QML approach is optimal
Limitations: Tested on only 3 small clinical datasets; IBMQ Melbourne now retired; hardware noise limits scalability; no large-scale clinical validation
Quantum Method Family: Quantum Kernel SVM / Quantum Distance Classifier
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – classical SVM and KNN compared
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Unclear – mixed results; competitive but not clearly superior

Title: Drug repurposing based on a quantum-inspired method versus classical fingerprinting uncovers potential antivirals against SARS-CoV-2
Author: Jose M. Jimenez-Guardeño; Ana Maria Ortega-Prieto; Borja Menendez Moreno; Thomas J. A. Maguire; Adam Richardson; Juan Ignacio Diaz-Hernandez; Javier Diez Perez; Mark Zuckerman; Albert Mercadal Playa; Carlos Cordero Deline; Michael H. Malim; Rocio Teresa Martinez-Nunez
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the need to identify new antiviral therapeutics through drug repurposing. A Quadratic Unbounded Binary Optimization (QUBO) model is employed on a quantum-inspired device to search for compounds similar to Remdesivir from the DrugBank database. Results are compared against traditional Tanimoto fingerprint model and validated in cell culture.
Method Used: QUBO model on quantum-inspired Fujitsu device; model Remdesivir and DrugBank compounds as graphs; solve Maximum Weighted Independent Set (MWIS) problem in conflict graph; compared to Tanimoto fingerprinting; IC50 validation in cell culture against SARS-CoV-2 variants; in vitro RdRP polymerization assay
Result: QUBO predicted GS-6620 (top) and BMS-986094 (second); Tanimoto predicted GS-6620 (top) and vitamin B12 forms; all predicted compounds inhibited replication of SARS-CoV-2 variants (Alpha, Beta, Delta) and directly inhibited RdRP
Conclusion: QUBO model performs accurate drug repurposing complementary to classical Tanimoto fingerprinting; quantum-inspired screening can accelerate drug deployment for complex pharmacological problems
Limitations: Quantum-inspired not true quantum computing; limited to compounds similar to Remdesivir scaffold; cell culture models may not fully predict in vivo efficacy; Tanimoto performed comparably for smaller searches
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Unclear – complementary to classical; not clearly superior

Title: EEG p-adic quantum potential accurately identifies depression schizophrenia and cognitive decline
Author: Oded Shor; Amir Glik; Amit Yaniv-Rosenfeld; Avi Valevski; Abraham Weizman; Andrei Khrennikov; Felix Benninger
Abstract: No accurate diagnostic tools exist for most neuropsychiatric disorders. A quantum potential mean and variability score (qpmvs) is developed to identify neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive disorders based on routine EEG recordings using p-adic numbers, Bohmian mechanics, and dendrogram representations. Evaluated on 230 participants including depression, schizophrenia, cognitive impairment, and controls.
Method Used: EEG recordings analyzed using quantum potential framework (Bohmian mechanics); ultrametric analysis with p-adic numbers and dendrogram trees; quantum potential mean and variability score (qpmvs) computed; AUC analysis with p-values for group separation
Result: High AUC for all group separations (all p<0.0001): healthy vs schizophrenia, depression, AD, MCI; schizophrenia vs depression, AD, MCI; depression vs AD and MCI
Conclusion: The qpmvs EEG algorithm is a useful and sufficiently accurate tool for diagnosis of neuropsychiatric and neurocognitive diseases and may predict disease course and response to treatment
Limitations: Small sample sizes per group (28 depression, 42 schizophrenia, 65 cognitive impairment, 95 controls); retrospective design; p-adic quantum analogy is theoretical not physical quantum computing; requires prospective validation
Classical Baseline Quality: No – no classical ML comparator reported

Title: Enhanced cardiovascular disease prediction through self-improved Aquila optimized feature selection in quantum neural network & LSTM model
Author: Aman Darolia; Rajender Singh Chhillar; Musaed Alhussein; Surjeet Dalal; Khursheed Aurangzeb; Umesh Kumar Lilhore
Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a pervasive cause of global mortality necessitating sophisticated prediction methodologies. This study presents a novel hybrid model for predicting CVD using self-improved Aquila optimization for optimal feature selection combined with a Quantum Neural Network and LSTM classifier evaluated on two datasets.
Method Used: Data preprocessing (missing/duplicate removal); feature extraction (central tendency, qualitative variation, dispersion, symmetrical uncertainty); self-improved Aquila optimization for feature selection; hybrid QNN+LSTM classification; algorithm to optimize LSTM weights; evaluated on two clinical CVD datasets
Result: Dataset-1: Accuracy 96.69%, Sensitivity 96.62%, Specificity 96.77%, Precision 96.03%, Recall 97.86%, F1 96.84%, MCC 96.37%, NPV 96.25%. Dataset-2: Accuracy 95.54%, Sensitivity 95.86%, Specificity 94.51%, Precision 96.03%, F1 96.94%, MCC 93.03%
Conclusion: Hybrid QNN-LSTM with Aquila feature selection accurately predicts CVD with improved precision over compared models; QNN and LSTM frameworks reveal cardiovascular risk-related physiological pathways
Limitations: Quantum components simulated not on real hardware; limited to tabular clinical datasets; no external clinical validation on independent cohorts; generalizability to diverse populations not established
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SVM, RF, LSTM, MLP compared
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, Precision, Recall, F1, MCC, NPV
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes – outperforms classical baselines on simulator

Title: Revolutionizing heart disease prediction with quantum-enhanced machine learning
Author: S. Venkatesh Babu; P. Ramya; Jeffin Gracewell
Abstract: This study evaluates Quantum Enhanced Machine Learning (QuEML) for heart disease prediction. The Kaggle heart disease dataset (1190 samples) is used to compare QuEML performance against traditional machine learning algorithms across accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 score, and training time.
Method Used: QuEML (quantum-enhanced ensemble approach) evaluated on Kaggle heart disease dataset (1190 samples, 53% positive/47% negative); performance compared against traditional ML algorithms; evaluated on accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, and training time
Result: QuEML accuracy 0.6% higher than classical ML; training time 192.5µs faster (670µs vs 862.5µs average); positive sample prediction rate 50.03% (QuEML) vs 49.78% (classical); negative prediction rate 44.65% (QuEML) vs 44.31% (classical)
Conclusion: QuEML is a promising approach in heart disease prediction with marginal accuracy improvement and faster training time compared to traditional ML; quantum computing can complement healthcare diagnostics
Limitations: Marginal improvement (0.6% accuracy); tested only on one Kaggle dataset; quantum components not run on real QPU; limited clinical validation; does not address real-world deployment challenges
Performance Metric(s) Reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Specificity, F1, Training time

Title: Quantum-inspired seagull optimised deep belief network approach for cardiovascular disease prediction
Author: D. Banumathy; T. Vetriselvi; K. Venkatachalam; Jaehyuk Cho
Abstract: The early detection and accurate diagnosis of cardiovascular diseases is vital to reduce global morbidity. This work proposes the quantum-inspired seagull optimization algorithm (QISOA) combined with a deep belief network (DBN) to improve identification of cardiovascular disorders. The publicly accessible Cleveland Heart Disease dataset is used for evaluation and comparison.
Method Used: Data preprocessing (cleaning, transformation, standardization); QISOA used to optimize weights and biases of DBN model; DBN for hierarchical feature learning and classification; quantum mechanics concepts enhance exploration; compared against SVM, DT, RF, MLP, FCN, PSO, GA, GWO, cuckoo search, crow search on Cleveland dataset
Result: QISOA-DBN: Accuracy 98.6%, Precision 97.6%, Recall 96.8%, F1 97.1%; outperforms all compared classical ML models and metaheuristic-based optimization models
Conclusion: QISOA-optimized DBN achieves superior cardiovascular disease prediction accuracy; quantum-inspired optimization effectively enhances DBN performance over classical and other metaheuristic baselines
Limitations: Evaluated only on Cleveland Heart Disease dataset; quantum-inspired not true quantum computing; limited generalizability to other cardiac datasets and populations; no real QPU validation
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SVM, DT, RF, MLP, PSO, GA, GWO compared
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes – outperforms classical and metaheuristic baselines

Title: Secretary bird optimization algorithm based on quantum computing and multiple strategies improvement for KELM diabetes classification
Author: Yu Zhu; Mingxu Zhang; Qinchuan Huang; Xianbo Wu; Li Wan; Ju Huang
Abstract: The classification of chronic diseases such as diabetes remains a critical research focus. This study introduces QHSBOA-KELM: an improved Secretary Bird Optimization Algorithm incorporating quantum computing-based t-distribution variations combined with Kernel Extreme Learning Machine for accurate diabetes classification prediction.
Method Used: SBOA enhanced with: particle swarm optimization search mechanism, dynamic boundary adjustments based on optimal individuals, and quantum computing-based t-distribution variations (QHSBOA); QHSBOA optimizes KELM kernel penalty C and bandwidth c; performance validated on CEC2017 benchmark; applied to diabetes datasets and compared against SBOA, PSO, and other optimization methods
Result: QHSBOA-KELM outperforms all compared models on four evaluation metrics: Accuracy (ACC), Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), sensitivity, and specificity across diabetes datasets
Conclusion: QHSBOA-KELM provides an effective method for early diagnosis and prediction of diabetes; quantum-inspired t-distribution variations improve optimizer exploration potential and convergence speed
Limitations: Quantum component is inspiration-only (t-distribution variations); no true quantum hardware used; tested on standard benchmark diabetes datasets; generalizability to diverse real-world clinical populations not assessed
Classical Baseline Quality: Yes – SBOA, PSO, other optimizers compared

Title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Transfer Learning for Cardiomegaly Detection in Chest X-rays
Author: Pierre Decoodt; Tan Jun Liang; Soham Bopardikar; Hemavathi Santhanam; Alfaxad Eyembe; Begonya Garcia-Zapirain; Daniel Sierra-Sosa
Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases may benefit from quantum machine learning advances in medical imaging. Hybrid classical-quantum (CQ) transfer learning models based on pre-trained DenseNet-121 are designed to detect cardiomegaly in chest X-rays (CXRs) using parameterized quantum circuits integrated via Qiskit and PennyLane. A balanced dataset of 2436 CXRs from CheXpert is used.
Method Used: Pre-trained DenseNet-121 + parameterized quantum circuit (PQC) integrated via Qiskit and PennyLane in PyTorch; CheXpert balanced dataset (2436 posteroanterior CXRs); k-fold cross-validation; state vector simulator; normalized global effective dimension for trainability; Grad-CAM++ heatmap visualization
Result: ROC AUC up to 0.93, accuracy up to 0.87 for several CQ models rivaling classical-classical (CC) DenseNet model; Grad-CAM++ hot zone covering heart: 94% (CQ) vs 61% (CC), p<0.001
Conclusion: Hybrid CQ transfer learning rivals classical DenseNet models for cardiomegaly detection; quantum circuits may enhance clinical interpretability through better Grad-CAM++ localization; promising for health professional acceptance
Limitations: Tested only on state vector simulator; no real QPU validation; balanced dataset may not reflect real clinical distribution; limited to binary cardiomegaly classification; small quantum circuit size
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Unclear – rivals classical model; no clear quantum advantage in accuracy

Title: Novel Hybrid Quantum Architecture-Based Lung Cancer Detection Using Chest Radiograph and Computerized Tomography Images
Author: Jason Elroy Martis; Sannidhan M S; Balasubramani R; A. M. Mutawa; M. Murugappan
Abstract: Lung cancer is the second most common cancer worldwide presenting significant health challenges. This study proposes a hybrid framework combining deep learning with quantum computing to enhance lung cancer detection accuracy using chest radiographs (CXR) and CT images. Pre-trained DL models are used for feature extraction and quantum circuits for classification.
Method Used: Pre-trained DL models for feature extraction from CXR and CT lung cancer images; hybrid quantum layers (parameterized quantum circuits) for classification; compared against classical DL models; evaluated on lung cancer CXR and CT datasets
Result: Overall accuracy 92.12%, sensitivity 94%, specificity 90%, F1 93%, precision 92%; outperforms traditional DL methods in accuracy, speed, and scalability
Conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical approach surpasses traditional methods in lung cancer detection; quantum computing enhances processing speed and scalability; promising tool for early lung cancer screening and improved patient care
Limitations: Quantum circuits simulated not on real QPU; dataset details not fully specified; no clinical deployment validation; improvement over classical DL marginal in some metrics; scalability to large clinical datasets not yet demonstrated
Quantum Advantage Claimed: Yes – outperforms traditional DL on simulator
